The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Assume AC. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one measurable space, with
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|,$$
the event-supremum convention without a factor $1/2$,
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}\le\sqrt{\frac12D(P\|Q)}.$$
If $P\not\ll Q$, the right side is $+\infty$ by the definition of KL
divergence.

derivations.claim: Fix one state $s$. Write $\Delta_a=q_s(a)-p_s(a)$; since both distributions have mass one, $\sum_a\Delta_a=0$. The set $B=\{a:\Delta_a\ge0\}$ consists of the nonnegative differences. The positive and negative parts of $\Delta$ therefore have equal sum, each equal to $\frac12\sum_a|\Delta_a|$. For every subset $C\subseteq A(s)$, $|\sum_{a\in C}\Delta_a|$ is at most this common sum, and $C=B$ attains it. Thus the event-supremum total variation in [F2] equals $\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)$.

Apply [F3] to the probability measures $q_s$ and $p_s$ on the finite power-set space, and use step 1.1. This gives $\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)\le\sqrt{D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)/2}$, including the infinite-divergence case.

If $K=+\infty$, the asserted inequality holds because each total-variation term is at most one. Suppose $K<\infty$ and put $m=K/2$. When $m=0$, step 2.1 gives $D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)\ge2\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)^2\ge0$ for every state. Since their $d$-weighted sum is zero, every state with $d(s)>0$ has zero divergence, so step 2.1 also gives zero total variation there. When $m>0$, for every $x\ge0$ the square $(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt m)^2\ge0$ gives $\sqrt{x}\le(\sqrt m+x/\sqrt m)/2$. Apply this with $x=D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)/2$ for states with $d(s)>0$, multiply by $d(s)$, and sum. Since $\sum_sd(s)=1$ and $\sum_sd(s)x_s=m$, the result is $\sum_sd(s)\sqrt{x_s}\le\sqrt m$. Step 2.1 now yields the claimed bound.

Let $M=(S,\mathcal R,(A(s))_{s\in S},p)$ be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state. Put $\mathcal X=\{(s,a,\rho,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ \rho\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$. Let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on $S$, let $\gamma\in[0,1)$, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and for each $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $b_i\in\mathbb R$, $C_i\ge0$, and $c_i:\mathcal X\to[-C_i,C_i]$. A **finite discounted constrained Markov decision process (CMDP)** is the tuple consisting of $M$, $\mu$, $\gamma$, and the bounded transition-cost functions and thresholds $(c_i,b_i)_{i=1}^m$. Its immediate reward signal is $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$.

For a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the state-mass sequence recursively by $\mu_0^\pi=\mu$ and

$$\mu_{t+1}^\pi(s'):=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a).$$

This recurrence defines nonnegative finite-time masses; the result that each $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution is established separately.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Let a finite discounted CMDP and a stationary policy $\pi$ be given. The **column transition matrix** $K_\pi$ has entry

$$K_\pi(s',s):=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a),$$

so that its column indexed by $s$ gives the next-state distribution from current state $s$. With the state-mass column vectors $\mu_t^\pi$ from the CMDP definition, the **normalized discounted state occupancy** is

$$d^\pi(s):=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\mu_t^\pi(s).$$

This normalization is part of the definition; the occupancy is a probability distribution by the separate well-definedness result below.

Let a finite discounted CMDP have initial distribution $\mu$, discount $\gamma\in[0,1)$, $m$ bounded transition signals $c_i$, thresholds $b_i$, and finite-time state masses $\mu_t^\pi$ under a stationary policy $\pi$, as defined in the CMDP model. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $M=(S,\mathcal R,(A(s))_{s\in S},p)$ be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state. Put $\mathcal X=\{(s,a,\rho,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ \rho\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$. A **finite discounted constrained Markov decision process (CMDP)** is the tuple consisting of $M$, $\mu$, $\gamma$, and the bounded transition-cost functions and thresholds $(c_i,b_i)_{i=1}^m$. Its immediate reward signal is $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$.

For a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the state-mass sequence recursively by $\mu_0^\pi=\mu$ and

$$\mu_{t+1}^\pi(s'):=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a).$$

This recurrence defines nonnegative finite-time masses; the result that each $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution is established separately.

Let a finite discounted CMDP have initial distribution $\mu$, discount $\gamma\in[0,1)$, $m$ bounded transition signals $c_i$, thresholds $b_i$, and finite-time state masses $\mu_t^\pi$ under a stationary policy $\pi$, as defined in the CMDP model. For any bounded transition signal $g$ on $(s,a,\rho,s')$, define its **expected discounted sum** under $\pi$ by

$$J_g^\pi(\mu):=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)g(s,a,\rho,s').$$

The expected discounted reward is $J^\pi:=J_r^\pi(\mu)$ for the immediate reward signal $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$, and the $i$th expected discounted cost is $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)$. The policy $\pi$ is **feasible** for the discounted-cost constraints exactly when $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)\le b_i$ for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Feasibility constrains these expectations; it does not assert a per-trajectory bound.

Let a finite discounted CMDP and a stationary policy $\pi$ be given. The **column transition matrix** $K_\pi$ has entry

$$K_\pi(s',s):=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a),$$

so that its column indexed by $s$ gives the next-state distribution from current state $s$. With the state-mass column vectors $\mu_t^\pi$ from the CMDP definition, the **normalized discounted state occupancy** is

$$d^\pi(s):=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\mu_t^\pi(s).$$

This normalization is part of the definition; the occupancy is a probability distribution by the separate well-definedness result below.

Let a finite discounted CMDP, a stationary policy $\pi$, its finite-time state-mass vectors $\mu_t^\pi$, its normalized discounted occupancy $d^\pi$, and the expected discounted signal $J_g^\pi(\mu)$ be as defined above. Each $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution, $d^\pi$ is a probability distribution, and for every bounded transition signal $g$ with $|g|\le B$, the series defining $J_g^\pi(\mu)$ converges absolutely and satisfies $|J_g^\pi(\mu)|\le B/(1-\gamma)$.

Put

Then the exact performance-difference identity is

$$J_g^{\pi'}(\mu)-J_g^\pi(\mu)=\frac{L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi')}{1-\gamma}+\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\sum_s\bigl(d^{\pi'}(s)-d^\pi(s)\bigr)\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s).$$

$$\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi):=\frac12\sum_{a\in A(s)}|\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)|$$

and $\|x\|_1:=\sum_{s\in S}|x(s)|$ for a state vector. Then

$$\|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1\le\frac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\sum_{s\in S}d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi).$$

$$\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s):=\frac12\sum_{a\in A(s)}|q_s(a)-p_s(a)|.$$

$$D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{a:q_s(a)>0}q_s(a)\log\frac{q_s(a)}{p_s(a)},&q_s(a)>0\Rightarrow p_s(a)>0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$

$$K:=\sum_{s:d(s)>0}d(s)D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)\in[0,+\infty].$$

where the right side is $+\infty$ when $K=+\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the theoretical average-KL comparison, and let a finite discounted CMDP have cost signals $c_1,\ldots,c_m$ with thresholds $b_1,\ldots,b_m$. Let $\theta\mapsto\pi_\theta$ be a stationary policy family on an open subset of $\mathbb R^d$ with fixed common support, and assume its policy coordinates are twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of the current parameter $\theta_k$. Choose a trust radius $\delta>0$, a backtracking factor $\beta\in(0,1)$, and a finite backtracking budget $L\ge0$. At iteration $k$, the finite data batch consists of $N\ge1$ rows $(s_j,a_j,\omega_j,\widehat A_j^r,\widehat A_{1,j}^c,\ldots,\widehat A_{m,j}^c)$ from trajectories generated in the CMDP under the current policy $\pi_{\theta_k}$, where $\omega_j\ge0$, $\sum_j\omega_j=1$, and $\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)>0$. The advantage estimates are real numbers held fixed during the update, and the batch also includes real baseline-cost estimates $\widehat J_{i,k}$. The weights and estimates may come from any fixed rollout or critic estimator; this procedure assumes no accuracy property for them. It specifies the exact finite-data trust-region subproblem and line search; implementations that approximate the subproblem solve are discussed separately.

For $\theta$ near $\theta_k$, define the finite sample surrogates

$$\widehat L_r(\theta):=\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\left(\frac{\pi_\theta(a_j\mid s_j)}{\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)}-1\right)\widehat A_j^r,\qquad \widehat L_i^c(\theta):=\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\left(\frac{\pi_\theta(a_j\mid s_j)}{\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)}-1\right)\widehat A_{i,j}^c.$$

and $\widehat K(\theta):=\sum_j\omega_jD_{\rm KL}(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s_j)\|\pi_{\theta_k}(\cdot\mid s_j))$. Put $g=\nabla\widehat L_r(\theta_k)$, $u_i=(1-\gamma)^{-1}\nabla\widehat L_i^c(\theta_k)$, $H=\nabla^2\widehat K(\theta_k)$, and $q_i=\widehat J_{i,k}-b_i$. The update procedure is:

1. If $H$ is not symmetric positive definite, meaning $x^THx>0$ for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^d$, return `no-step`. Otherwise form the local quadratic program

   $$\max_{x\in\mathbb R^d} g^Tx\quad\text{subject to}\quad q_i+u_i^Tx\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \frac12x^THx\le\delta.$$

2. If this program is feasible, let $x^*$ be its lexicographically least global maximizer. The feasible set is a closed subset of the compact ellipsoid, so the maximizer set is nonempty and compact. Minimize the first coordinate on that set, restrict to its nonempty compact minimizers, and repeat for each coordinate; the resulting point is the lexicographically least maximizer. If the program is infeasible and $m=1$, compute $v=H^{-1}u_1$. If $u_1=0$, return `no-step`, since the linearized cost cannot be reduced. Otherwise $u_1^Tv>0$ by positive definiteness, and use the cost-recovery proposal $x^*=-\sqrt{2\delta/(u_1^Tv)}\,v$. If the program is infeasible and $m>1$, return `no-step`.

3. For $j=0,\ldots,L$, set $\theta_j=\theta_k+\beta^jx^*$. Accept the first $\theta_j$ in the policy family's parameter domain for which $\widehat K(\theta_j)\le\delta$ and every sample cost estimate $\widehat J_{i,k}+(1-\gamma)^{-1}\widehat L_i^c(\theta_j)$ is at most $b_i$. If no candidate passes this sample check, return `no-step`; otherwise output the accepted parameter as $\theta_{k+1}$.

For finite constants $D_i\ge0$, optional nonnegative bounded transition signals $\Delta_i:\mathcal X\to[0,D_i]$ may be included in the supplied cost-advantage and baseline estimates by estimating the shaped costs $c_i+\Delta_i$. The exact theorem concerns exact policies and expectations; the line search above checks only the supplied sample estimates.

Let a finite discounted CMDP, a bounded transition signal $g$, a bounded function $f:S\to\mathbb R$, and stationary policies $\pi,\pi'$ be given. For each state define

$$\bar\delta_f^{g,\sigma}(s):=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}\sigma(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\bigl(g(s,a,\rho,s')+\gamma f(s')-f(s)\bigr),\qquad \sigma\in\{\pi,\pi'\}.$$

Set $\epsilon_f^g(\pi'):=\max_{s\in S}|\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)|$ and

$$L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi'):=\sum_{s\in S}d^\pi(s)\bigl(\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)-\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi}(s)\bigr),\qquad D_{\pi,f}^{\pm,g}(\pi'):=\frac{L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi')}{1-\gamma}\pm\frac{2\gamma\epsilon_f^g(\pi')}{(1-\gamma)^2}\sum_{s\in S}d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi),$$

where $\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi):=\frac12\sum_{a\in A(s)}|\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)|$. Then

$$D_{\pi,f}^{-,g}(\pi')\le J_g^{\pi'}(\mu)-J_g^\pi(\mu)\le D_{\pi,f}^{+,g}(\pi').$$

These total-variation bounds are choice-free. Under the additional Axiom of Choice, define

$$\overline D_{\rm KL}^{\pi}(\pi'\|\pi):=\sum_{s:d^\pi(s)>0}d^\pi(s)D_{\rm KL}\bigl(\pi'(\cdot\mid s)\|\pi(\cdot\mid s)\bigr),$$

using natural logarithms and $+\infty$ when the first action law is not absolutely continuous with respect to the second. The same inequalities hold after replacing $\sum_s d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi)$ by $\sqrt{\overline D_{\rm KL}^{\pi}(\pi'\|\pi)/2}$; when the average KL is infinite, these KL-form inequalities are interpreted as the trivial extended bounds $-\infty\le J_g^{\pi'}(\mu)-J_g^\pi(\mu)\le+\infty$. Taking $g=r$ gives the reward bound, and taking $g=c_i$ gives the corresponding bound for each discounted cost.

$$J_g^\pi(\mu):=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)g(s,a,\rho,s').$$

The expected discounted reward is $J^\pi:=J_r^\pi(\mu)$ for the immediate reward signal $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$, and the $i$th expected discounted cost is $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)$. The policy $\pi$ is **feasible** for the discounted-cost constraints exactly when $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)\le b_i$ for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Feasibility constrains these expectations; it does not assert a per-trajectory bound.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the theoretical average-KL comparison, and let a finite discounted CMDP have cost signals $c_1,\ldots,c_m$ with thresholds $b_1,\ldots,b_m$. Let $\theta\mapsto\pi_\theta$ be a stationary policy family on an open subset of $\mathbb R^d$ with fixed common support, and assume its policy coordinates are twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of the current parameter $\theta_k$. Choose a trust radius $\delta>0$, a backtracking factor $\beta\in(0,1)$, and a finite backtracking budget $L\ge0$. At iteration $k$, the finite data batch consists of $N\ge1$ rows $(s_j,a_j,\omega_j,\widehat A_j^r,\widehat A_{1,j}^c,\ldots,\widehat A_{m,j}^c)$ from trajectories generated in the CMDP under the current policy $\pi_{\theta_k}$, where $\omega_j\ge0$, $\sum_j\omega_j=1$, and $\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)>0$. The advantage estimates are real numbers held fixed during the update, and the batch also includes real baseline-cost estimates $\widehat J_{i,k}$. The weights and estimates may come from any fixed rollout or critic estimator; this procedure assumes no accuracy property for them. It specifies the exact finite-data trust-region subproblem and line search; implementations that approximate the subproblem solve are discussed separately.

For $\theta$ near $\theta_k$, define the finite sample surrogates

$$\widehat L_r(\theta):=\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\left(\frac{\pi_\theta(a_j\mid s_j)}{\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)}-1\right)\widehat A_j^r,\qquad \widehat L_i^c(\theta):=\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\left(\frac{\pi_\theta(a_j\mid s_j)}{\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)}-1\right)\widehat A_{i,j}^c.$$

and $\widehat K(\theta):=\sum_j\omega_jD_{\rm KL}(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s_j)\|\pi_{\theta_k}(\cdot\mid s_j))$. Put $g=\nabla\widehat L_r(\theta_k)$, $u_i=(1-\gamma)^{-1}\nabla\widehat L_i^c(\theta_k)$, $H=\nabla^2\widehat K(\theta_k)$, and $q_i=\widehat J_{i,k}-b_i$. The update procedure is:

1. If $H$ is not symmetric positive definite, meaning $x^THx>0$ for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^d$, return `no-step`. Otherwise form the local quadratic program

   $$\max_{x\in\mathbb R^d} g^Tx\quad\text{subject to}\quad q_i+u_i^Tx\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \frac12x^THx\le\delta.$$

2. If this program is feasible, let $x^*$ be its lexicographically least global maximizer. The feasible set is a closed subset of the compact ellipsoid, so the maximizer set is nonempty and compact. Minimize the first coordinate on that set, restrict to its nonempty compact minimizers, and repeat for each coordinate; the resulting point is the lexicographically least maximizer. If the program is infeasible and $m=1$, compute $v=H^{-1}u_1$. If $u_1=0$, return `no-step`, since the linearized cost cannot be reduced. Otherwise $u_1^Tv>0$ by positive definiteness, and use the cost-recovery proposal $x^*=-\sqrt{2\delta/(u_1^Tv)}\,v$. If the program is infeasible and $m>1$, return `no-step`.

3. For $j=0,\ldots,L$, set $\theta_j=\theta_k+\beta^jx^*$. Accept the first $\theta_j$ in the policy family's parameter domain for which $\widehat K(\theta_j)\le\delta$ and every sample cost estimate $\widehat J_{i,k}+(1-\gamma)^{-1}\widehat L_i^c(\theta_j)$ is at most $b_i$. If no candidate passes this sample check, return `no-step`; otherwise output the accepted parameter as $\theta_{k+1}$.

For finite constants $D_i\ge0$, optional nonnegative bounded transition signals $\Delta_i:\mathcal X\to[0,D_i]$ may be included in the supplied cost-advantage and baseline estimates by estimating the shaped costs $c_i+\Delta_i$. The exact theorem concerns exact policies and expectations; the line search above checks only the supplied sample estimates.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $q$ be a positive definite quadratic form on $\mathbb R^n$. Then some $c>0$ satisfies $q(u)\ge c$ whenever $\|u\|_2=1$. For a negative definite $q$, some $c>0$ satisfies $q(u)\le-c$ on the same sphere.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $F \subseteq X$ be closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$: the metric
subspace $(F, d_F)$ is a compact metric space
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: First consider $d\ge1$ and symmetric positive definite $H$. By homogeneity, [F2] gives $x^THx\ge c\|x\|_2^2$ for all $x$, with zero handled directly. Put $C=\sum_{a,b}|H_{ab}|$. Coordinate bounds in [F6] and the identity $x_ax_b-y_ay_b=(x_a-y_a)x_b+y_a(x_b-y_b)$ give $|x^THx-y^THy|\le C\|x-y\|_2(\|x\|_2+\|y\|_2)$, so the quadratic form is continuous. The ellipsoid $E=\{x:x^THx/2\le\delta\}$ is therefore closed and contained in the ball of radius $\sqrt{2\delta/c}$, hence compact by [F3]. Each linear functional $x\mapsto v^Tx$ is continuous because $|v^T(x-y)|\le\|v\|_2\|x-y\|_2$. Thus the feasible set $F=E\cap\bigcap_i\{x:q_i+u_i^Tx\le0\}$ is a closed subset of $E$, and is compact.

If $F$ is nonempty, [F4] gives an attained maximum $M$ of $g^Tx$ on $F$. Its maximizer set $K_0=\{x\in F:g^Tx=M\}$ is nonempty and compact by closedness and [F3]. Successively for coordinates $h=1,\ldots,d$, let $a_h$ be the minimum of coordinate $h$ on $K_{h-1}$ and set $K_h=\{x\in K_{h-1}:x_h=a_h\}$. Each minimum exists by [F4], and each restriction remains nonempty and compact by [F3]. After $d$ restrictions all coordinates are fixed, so $K_d$ is a singleton. For any other maximizer, the first coordinate where it differs from this singleton must be greater, by the construction of that coordinate's minimum. The singleton is therefore exactly the unique lexicographically least maximizer. As a member of $F$, it satisfies all stated constraints.

If $Hz=0$, then $z^THz=0$ and positive definiteness forces $z=0$. Thus [F5] supplies $H^{-1}$. In the single-cost recovery branch write $u=u_1\ne0$, $v=H^{-1}u$. Then $v\ne0$, $Hv=u$ and $a=u^Tv=v^THv>0$. For every $x\in E$, nonnegativity of the quadratic form at $x-(u^Tx/a)v$ gives $0\le x^THx-(u^Tx)^2/a$, using symmetry. Consequently $u^Tx\ge-\sqrt{2\delta a}$. For $x^*=-\sqrt{2\delta/a}\,v$, direct substitution gives $(x^*)^THx^*=2\delta$ and $u^Tx^*=-\sqrt{2\delta a}$, attaining the bound. If another point attains it, equality in the preceding inequalities gives $(x-(u^Tx/a)v)^TH(x-(u^Tx/a)v)=0$, hence $x=(u^Tx/a)v=x^*$ by positive definiteness. The recovery proposal is therefore unique, and its linearized cost is $q_1-\sqrt{2\delta a}$. Since it is the minimum over $E$, infeasibility implies that this last value is strictly positive, rather than implying feasibility.

The remaining proposal branches are the explicit returns in [F1]: non-positive-definite $H$, infeasible single-cost problem with $u_1=0$, and infeasible problem with $m>1$ all return `no-step`. If $d=0$, the only parameter displacement is the zero vector, so a feasible program has that unique maximizer, and in the infeasible case all $u_i=0$ and one of the specified no-step branches applies. Thus zero dimension introduces no missing proposal case. Together with steps 2.1 and 2.2, every branch either gives one uniquely specified proposal or returns `no-step`.

For a proposal $x^*$, the candidates $\theta_k+\beta^jx^*$ for integer $j=0,\ldots,L$ form a prescribed ordered list of $L+1$ points. The parameter-domain check precedes evaluation of the policy tests, so no value outside the domain is required. On the domain, the finite common-support policy probabilities define the empirical KL and surrogates in [F1]. Either there is a least passing index in this finite list, or there is none; [F1] returns its candidate or `no-step`, respectively. Inspecting successive indices therefore terminates in at most $L+1$ candidate tests. The definition of passing supplies exactly the stated sample inequalities. All choices and returns are single-valued by steps 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1 and this least-index rule, establishing the asserted output and finite-search properties. No step in this argument compares the sample estimates to population expectations.
